STRIDE / EVIDENCE-LED DEVELOPMENT

From motion tracking to meaningful feedback.

People can track how much they walk, but have limited opportunities to understand and respond to how they walk in real time. STRIDE explores a more actionable walking experience — without claiming to diagnose or correct posture.

01 / NOW
WORKING PROTOTYPE

Phone-based tracking

Experimental step and cadence estimates, rule-based audio prompts and browser-local session history. No shoe sensors connected.

02 / NEXT
RESEARCH HYPOTHESIS

Does feedback help?

Compare estimated steps with manual counts; study whether feedback changes consistency across repeated walks. Not yet validated.

03 / FUTURE
DESIGN CONCEPT

Cloudmuse footwear

Fashion-led sneaker with proposed pressure sensing, motion hardware and wireless connectivity. Hardware feasibility untested.

STRIDE / RESEARCH & EVIDENCE

What works. What we test. What comes next.

Transparent evidence boundaries for an experimental fashion × motion prototype. / 현재 구현, 연구 검증, 미래 제품을 분리합니다.

01 / CURRENT
IMPLEMENTED · NOT VALIDATED

Smartphone prototype

Motion readings, heuristic step detection, cadence estimates, rule-based voice cues, session history. Results depend on device, placement and browser support.

02 / STUDY
PLANNED · NO CLAIMED RESULTS

Feedback effectiveness

Compare repeated walks with and without audio prompts. Evaluate rhythm consistency and user experience; this is a hypothesis, not a demonstrated outcome.

03 / PRODUCT
CONCEPT · NO HARDWARE

Cloudmuse sneaker

Conceptual pressure-sensor insole, IMU, BLE and everyday footwear design. The 3D pressure markers are illustrations, not measurements.

What each metric can actually tell us

Signal / featureCurrent interpretationNot established
Phone accelerometerPhone movement and experimental step detectionFoot pressure, pelvic position, spinal alignment
Cadence / step intervalsEstimated walking rhythm under consistent phone placementClinical gait quality or diagnosis
Rule-based voice promptsMessages triggered by predefined heuristicsVerified improvement in gait or posture
3D sensor visualizationFuture hardware design communicationLive in-shoe sensing or calibrated force values

01 — Step-count validation lab

Walk a known number of steps while keeping the phone in the same location. Enter your manually counted steps and STRIDE's estimated steps. This tool stores a comparison on this browser only; it does not prove clinical accuracy.

02 — Coaching-effect study protocol

A / Baseline

Walk a fixed route at a comfortable pace without audio cues. Record device placement, estimated cadence and step-interval variability.

B / Feedback

Repeat under similar conditions with rule-based prompts enabled. Keep route, phone placement and duration comparable.

C / Compare

Compare repeated trials and note user comfort, perceived usefulness and variability. A change is not proof of medical correction.

Study design only. No controlled trial, clinical validation, sensor calibration or demonstrated therapeutic benefit is claimed. A credible study needs repeated observations and clear limitations.

03 — Footwear system roadmap

PHASE 1 / TODAY

Web app

Phone motion → heuristic detection → rule-based feedback → local session records.

PHASE 2 / PROTOTYPE

Instrumented insole

Proposed pressure sensors + IMU → microcontroller + BLE → phone app. Requires power, durability and calibration work.

PHASE 3 / EVALUATION

Wearability & evidence

Test comfort, washability, battery life, signal quality, repeatability and user outcomes before product claims.

Competitive positioning — hypotheses to test

ReferenceRelevant capabilitySTRIDE design question
Apple HealthEstablished iPhone walking metricsWhat incremental value does an actionable coaching experience provide?
Moticon OpenGoInstrumented insole and gait-related sensingCan hardware be made wearable as everyday fashion?
Other gait-tracking appsPhone-derived gait indicators and chartsDoes the feedback and footwear experience improve retention or usefulness?

Positioning is a research hypothesis; STRIDE does not claim to be first or clinically superior.
